e.t: Hur is a Hebrew personal name, identifying a man called “Hur” rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its ordinary function is as a name used to distinguish a particular person. This name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in 1 Kings 4:8. The available wording consistently supports “Hur,” while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s specific role in the passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “revilings”—words spoken against someone in a hostile, insulting way. It functions as a noun, naming the verbal abuse or contempt directed toward a person or people. It appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 43:28, Isaiah 51:7, and Zephaniah 2:8. In Isaiah 51:7, it is connected with people hearing, knowing, fearing, and being reproached, showing its place in language about opposition directed at God’s people.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “captivity,” the condition of people being taken away and held under another power. It can describe the state of those removed from their land or community, rather than the act of taking them. In the Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, especially in passages concerning Israel and other peoples being carried away. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Ahava is a proper place name, referring to the location called “Ahava.” It is not presented here as an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Ezra 8:15, 8:21, and 8:31. The English rendering preserves it as “Ahava,” so its identifiable sense is the name of a specific place rather than a broader lexical idea.

This Hebrew word refers to “showers.” It functions as the predicate of a statement, describing what is associated with God in its only Old Testament occurrence, Jeremiah 14:22. Because it appears only once, its meaning is limited to this single recorded use, but the rendering clearly presents the word as an action or provision involving showers rather than as a person, place, or object. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding biblical text.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name Delilah, referring to the woman who appears in Judges 16. It functions as a proper name rather than as a general description or action word. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Judges 16:4–18. Its recorded uses are connected with spoken exchanges involving Delilah, especially her repeated dealings with Samson. Because it is a name, its meaning in any particular sentence comes chiefly from identifying the person being mentioned, while the surrounding passage supplies the details of her actions and character.

This Hebrew word means “innocency.” It names a condition associated with a person, rather than an action, object, or place. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 6:22, so its normal lexical range cannot be broadened from repeated uses. The occurrence identifies the word’s rendering but does not provide the surrounding verse text; the passage context therefore determines its precise force there.

This Hebrew verb means “hide”—to conceal oneself or remain out of sight. It describes the act of withdrawing from view, whether a person is hidden or something is kept concealed. The word occurs 33 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a repeated biblical use for hiding or being hidden. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word expresses “joined.” It functions as an action word, describing joining rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 4:12. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be stated beyond this basic sense. The normal meaning remains the act expressed by “joined.”

This Hebrew verb means “pass,” describing an action rather than a person, place, or object. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel 4. In each available English rendering, it is represented by “pass,” supporting a consistent central sense. The word presents something as moving onward or crossing from one point or time to another; the surrounding sentence determines the exact aspect of that action.

This Hebrew word means “flatteries,” referring to praise or approval offered in a pleasing but insincere way. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 11:32. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to flattering speech or conduct rather than genuine faithfulness. The rendering “flatteries” captures its central sense without requiring a broader range of meanings.

This word is a place name, rendered “Hazar” or “Shual.” It identifies a settlement in the Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name occurs eight times in four verses, appearing in Joshua, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Its references place it among recorded towns and settlements, so its ordinary function is geographic: it names a specific location. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that location’s role in each passage.

This Hebrew word means “sickle,” a hand tool used to cut or reap grain. It names a physical implement rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Deuteronomy: 16:9 and 23:25. Its repeated rendering as “sickle” supports this ordinary meaning. The word therefore refers to the curved cutting tool associated with gathering standing grain. The surrounding verse determines the specific instruction involving it.

This Hebrew word describes slaughtering or killing, especially the taking of life in a violent act. It is rendered with the meaning “slaughter” and, in some aligned passages, is associated with “men.” Across its 11 Old Testament occurrences, it is used in settings involving people or animals being killed, including language about slaughtered sheep and slain persons. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. Evidence comes from its recorded Old Testament references and meaning candidates.

Igdaliah is a Hebrew personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 35:4, and is rendered “Igdaliah.” Because it functions as a name, its ordinary meaning here is the person it identifies. The surrounding verse context would be needed to explain that individual’s role in the passage.

Achmetha is a proper place name, referring to a specific location rather than expressing an action, quality, or common object. It appears once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in Ezra 6:2. Because the word functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identifying: it designates the place called “Achmetha.” The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular role in that passage, but the word itself serves as a geographical name.

This Hebrew word means “sweep.” It expresses an action of sweeping something away or across an area. In its one Old Testament occurrence, it functions as the action being described rather than as a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in Isaiah 28:17 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s central sense is the movement of sweeping. It is rendered “sweep” in the available English renderings.

Jaroah is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as the identifying name of an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 5:14. Because it is a name, its ordinary role is to identify the person being mentioned; the name itself does not provide a broader meaning in the available biblical wording. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in the genealogy or list.

This Hebrew word refers to a “sieve,” a tool used to separate or sift material. Its meaning is straightforward and concrete rather than describing an action, emotion, or abstract quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Amos 9:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this summary gives the word’s ordinary meaning without assigning additional details to its use in that passage.

Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its ordinary function is to identify talents as a recognized measure or amount.

e.t: “Levi” is a Hebrew proper name referring to Levi, the son of Jacob, and to the family or tribe descended from him. It is used in genealogical settings and in passages involving the Levites’ place among Israel and their service before the LORD. The name occurs 64 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi. Its references commonly identify Levi or his descendants rather than describe an action or quality.

This Hebrew word refers to “concubines,” functioning as a plural noun for the women identified in the account. It occurs three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, all in Daniel 5:2, 5:3, and 5:23. The wording consistently identifies this group as distinct from the king’s wives and other people present. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and the actions or relationships described there.

Magog is a proper name used in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies a figure in genealogical records and is also named in Ezekiel’s prophetic passages. The word occurs four times, at Genesis 10:2, 1 Chronicles 1:5, Ezekiel 38:2, and Ezekiel 39:6. In the English renderings, it consistently appears as “Magog,” so its meaning is the name itself rather than a general descriptive term.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “savoury” food or prepared dishes. It functions as the object of actions involving preparation, taking, bringing, and giving. In its eight Old Testament occurrences, it is especially associated with the food prepared and served in Genesis 27, while it also appears in Proverbs. The word therefore identifies a prepared food item valued for its taste and presented to another person. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “angel,” referring to a heavenly messenger or servant of God. It is a noun used for a spiritual being whom God sends to act on behalf of His purposes. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word appears twice, both in Daniel: once in Daniel 3:28 and once in Daniel 6:22. Its basic meaning identifies the being involved, while the surrounding verse explains what that angel does in each passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “perfection.” It functions as a noun, naming a quality or condition rather than describing an action. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 15:29. Because it appears only once and no surrounding verse text is available here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be expanded beyond this basic meaning. The word’s central sense is therefore the condition identified as “perfection.”

Across its 20 Old Testament occurrences, the word remains centered on these rival objects of devotion. Related passages place such idols in settings of bowing before them and commands concerning them. Thus, the word names an idol as an object of religious trust or worship, rather than the living God.

Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains connected with holding or enclosing.

e.t: This word is a personal name, rendered “Abiram.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, chiefly in the account of the rebellion connected with Korah and in later references to that event. Because it is a name, its specific reference depends on the surrounding passage; the word itself functions as the person’s identifying designation.

Marsena is a personal name, referring to one of the officials associated with the Persian king’s court. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 1:14, and is rendered “Marsena.” Because this word is a proper name rather than a common noun or descriptive term, its meaning lies chiefly in identifying the individual who bears it. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role in the passage.

This word refers to “Mithnite,” a personal designation preserved in English Bible translations. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 11:43, and functions as an identifying name rather than a general description or action. The available wording does not provide a broader lexical definition, so its clearest meaning is the name “Mithnite.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being identified there.

This Hebrew word expresses the action of making something “void”—treating it as no longer effective, honored, or operative. It is a rare Old Testament word, occurring twice in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 89:39 and Lamentations 2:7. Its basic sense focuses on the removal or rejection of something’s established standing or function. The surrounding sentence determines exactly what has been made void in each occurrence, but the central idea remains the same: something is deprived of its recognized force or place.

This Hebrew word refers to “taskmasters,” people who impose or oversee demanding labor. It functions as a noun identifying those who press others to fulfill required work. In the Old Testament, it occurs 23 times, especially in passages concerning Israel’s forced labor in Egypt. It also appears in later passages, showing that the word’s central idea remains associated with pressure placed upon people through imposed demands.

This Hebrew verb means “take,” describing the action of taking someone or something. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in two verses in Daniel. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being taken and how the surrounding words describe the action.

This Hebrew verb describes a person’s state or action, appearing in English as “is” or “played.” As “is,” it functions as a statement about what someone is; as “played,” it describes what someone did. It occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears. The word is found in passages from Genesis, Samuel, Chronicles, and Isaiah, showing that it can serve in more than one sentence pattern while retaining its role as a verb.

This Hebrew verb means “Take,” expressing an action directed toward receiving or carrying something in a sentence. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Judges 19:30 and Isaiah 8:10. The word functions as an action word rather than a name or description. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is a direct instruction or statement about taking.

Iram is a personal name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Genesis 36:43 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:54. Both occurrences render the name as “Iram.” Because the passages do not provide a separate definition or description of the name itself, its meaning here is its identifying function: it distinguishes a particular individual in biblical genealogical lists.

This Hebrew verb means “complain”: to express dissatisfaction or protest in words. It describes a person voicing a grievance rather than simply feeling troubled silently. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Numbers and once in Lamentations, showing its use for expressed complaint in different settings. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains an expressed complaint. It functions as an action word describing what someone says or does.

This Hebrew word describes something as “durable”—able to remain sound and useful rather than quickly wearing out. It functions as a descriptive word applied to a thing or quality, focusing on its lasting strength or usefulness. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 23:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea is durability: something dependable for continued use.

The word occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force in a sentence depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “dark,” describing a condition of little or no light. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Amos 5:20, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “copy”—a written version given, delivered, or made available to others. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra and Esther. Its uses are connected with giving or presenting a copy and with commands communicated through it, so the word identifies the written item being passed on rather than the person issuing the command. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word describes something as “thirsty,” indicating a condition marked by a need for water. It functions as a description of a dry or water-lacking state rather than naming a person or action. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its scriptural use is associated with water and places affected by its absence, while Isaiah also connects it with a future change involving water.

“Zarthan” is a proper place name in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies a location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs three times, in Joshua and 1 Kings, and appears in passages describing people or rulers in relation to that place. Its precise geographical location is not established by the available wording here, but its function as a named location is clear.

This Hebrew word means “before.” It marks a person, thing, or situation as being in front of, or in the presence of, another. It occurs 46 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Daniel and Ezra. In its sentences, it commonly identifies where someone stands or to whom something is presented. Its basic function is relational: it places one person or thing before another rather than describing an action or quality.

This Hebrew word means “assembled.” It is a verb describing people as being brought into one group, rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament it occurs 39 times, making it a recurring word for the formation of a group. The surrounding sentence determines who is assembled and why, but the word itself centers on people being brought together as one collective body.

The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its consistent rendering as “Riblah” confirms its proper-name function. Several recorded connections place Riblah in accounts involving kings and their movements or dealings, showing that it serves as a geographical reference within those historical narratives.

This Hebrew word refers chiefly to “cedar,” a noun associated with the cedar tree or its wood. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 27:24. The available renderings also include “made,” so its precise wording in that occurrence depends on how the surrounding phrase is understood. Its central lexical idea is best retained as “cedar,” while the single occurrence does not provide enough context to explain a broader figurative or spiritual use.

Rinnah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Rinnah.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the queen’s place in the royal setting.
